claims.text: The starting material is an equimolar CoCrFeNiTi elemental powder mixture.
Approximately 6 hours of high-energy ball milling will generate a critical level of lattice strain and grain refinement in CoCrFeNiTi.
Six-hour milling will produce a high dislocation density and nanocrystalline grain size.
Milling-induced strain and grain refinement increase the stored energy and lower the barrier for a BCC-to-FCC transition.
The relevant transition in CoCrFeNiTi is from a metastable BCC solid solution to a stable FCC solid solution.
The CoCrFeNiTi alloy has a VEC of approximately 8.0–8.5.
VEC and atomic-radius mismatch govern the stability of the proposed FCC/BCC transition, with high Ti content tending to favor BCC.
SPS at 1000°C, 10 MPa for 10 minutes will provide sufficient atomic diffusion for densification.
SPS at 1000°C remains below the critical temperature for excessive Ti-driven HCP precipitation.
Ti segregation and reduced stacking-fault energy at higher temperatures drive HCP formation in CoCrFeNiTi.
Approximately 1100°C is the upper sintering-temperature boundary beyond which grain growth becomes dominant.
Above approximately 1100°C, HCP decomposition is expected to dominate.
The proposed process will produce a fully dense alloy with porosity below 2%.
The processed alloy will have a dominant FCC solid solution and no significant HCP precipitation.
Vickers hardness will increase by more than 40% relative to cast CoCrFeNiTi.
The final grain size will be below 500 nm.
Cast CoCrFeNiTi has low hardness, high porosity, and may contain brittle intermetallic phases.
Milling beyond 8 hours risks excessive contamination or amorphization that hinders sintering.
Oxygen content can shift the threshold for HCP precipitation and the optimum milling duration.
Vickers hardness testing at a 100 g load can isolate grain-boundary strengthening from precipitation hardening.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis and boundary treat temperatures above the limit as promoting excessive HCP precipitation, whereas the mechanism says that HCP decomposition dominates above approximately 1100°C. Precipitation and decomposition imply opposite changes in HCP phase fraction.
